books.section: Topic 8.10 The African-American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)
The Civil Rights Movement in the 1960s: From Integration to Black Power

source: original; stimulus photograph viewed before writing

stimulus.source_note: Photograph: President Lyndon Johnson signing the Voting Rights Act, August 6, 1965, public domain (U.S. federal government photograph via Wikimedia Commons). Account drawn from the grounding books (Barron's Ch. 10, Topic 8.10, "The Selma to Montgomery March (1965)" and "The Voting Rights Act (1965)"; 5 Steps Ch. 27; Princeton Ch. 12). The March 7 and March 15, 1965 dates are in the books; the registration table is from the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, Political Participation (1968), as summarized in the EBSCO research starter on the act.
stimulus.text:
The photograph shows President Lyndon Johnson signing the Voting Rights Act on August 6, 1965, with Martin Luther King Jr. standing behind him. The act followed the Selma campaign for voting rights. On March 7, 1965, marchers crossing the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, were attacked by state and county police with clubs and tear gas in an event known as Bloody Sunday; television carried the attack across the country. On March 15 Johnson addressed Congress in support of voting rights, saying, "We shall overcome." The march from Selma to Montgomery was completed later that month. The Voting Rights Act outlawed literacy tests and authorized federal examiners to register voters in places where few Black citizens were registered. It also required places with a history of discrimination to get federal approval before changing their voting laws.

African American voter registration, percent of voting-age population (U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, 1968):

| State | 1964 | 1967 |
| Mississippi | 6.7% | 59.8% |
| Alabama | 23.0% | 51.6% |
| Georgia | 27.4% | 52.6% |
| Louisiana | 31.6% | 58.9% |
| South Carolina | 37.3% | 51.2% |
| Virginia | 38.3% | 55.6% |

stem: The Voting Rights Act's use of federal examiners and federal approval for voting-law changes most directly shows which shift?

options.text: Voting rights were left entirely to state governments to enforce
options.misconception: Federal examiners and federal approval mean Washington enforced the law, not the states alone.

options.text: The federal government took over running all elections in the United States
options.misconception: The act applied federal oversight where discrimination had blocked registration, not to every election.

options.text: Enforcement moved from waiting for court cases to direct federal action
Literacy tests were kept in place but made easier to pass
options.misconception: The passage says the act outlawed literacy tests.

rationales.A: Federal examiners registered voters themselves, so enforcement was not left to the states.
rationales.B: The act targeted places where few Black citizens were registered, not every election in the country.
rationales.C: The passage says the act sent federal examiners to register voters and required federal approval before voting laws could change.
rationales.D: The passage says the act outlawed literacy tests, not that it kept them.
rationales.general:
1. Background: Before the act, Black citizens had to fight each barrier in court, one case at a time.
2. The act outlawed literacy tests outright.
3. It sent federal examiners to register voters where few Black citizens were registered.
4. It required federal approval before voting laws could change in those places.
Remember: A law that sends its own officers enforces itself instead of waiting for lawsuits.
